title: Building a Smarter AI Agent with Neural RAG - Will Bryk, Exa.ai

primary.label: Retrieval, Search & Knowledge

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's core subject is Exa's neural search engine built on document embeddings, hybrid retrieval, and RAG architecture for AI agents. Exa is a search and knowledge retrieval API serving developer platforms such as Cursor, Databricks, and LlamaIndex. Exa is a live production system launched in November 2022 with active enterprise customers and a newly announced research endpoint. Prerequisites include familiarity with RAG, embeddings, transformers, and Python for agent code, targeting practitioners with foundational AI knowledge. Recorded conference talk at the AI Engineer World's Fair featuring live coding demonstrations of search and agent applications. All evidence anchors are direct excerpts from the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Will Bryk opens with a narrative framing: the story ends with "one API to get any information from the web." He traces Google's 1998 PageRank, which ranked documents by authority but relied on keyword comparison. By 2021, Bryk noticed GPT-3 understood nuanced language while Google failed on "shirts without stripes," exposing keyword search's inability to understand negation. Exa joined YC Summer 2021, raised a couple million dollars, spent half on a GPU cluster, and did research for 1.5 years without talking to users. The core idea replaced traditional keyword inverted indexes with transformer-generated document embeddings capturing meaning, ideas, and reference patterns. At search time, the query is embedded and compared against all document embeddings. After training breakthroughs, Exa launched November 2022; ChatGPT launched two weeks later, ultimately validating the need for AI-native search via an information-theory argument: GPT-4's weights are under 10 TB while the web exceeds a million TB and constantly updates. Traditional search engines were built for lazy humans who type simple keywords and want a few links. AI agents are fundamentally different: they carry large accumulated context, use complex multi-constraint queries, want comprehensive knowledge (processing 10,000 pages in seconds), and need results that return exactly what is asked rather than what humans tend to click. Bryk maps the expanding query space: pre-2022 keyword queries, post-2022 LLM-style queries, semantic queries like "people in San Francisco who know assembly," and complex filtered queries that turn the web into a database. He then live-codes demos: a search dashboard exposing toggles for result count, date ranges, domain filters, and neural vs keyword modes; an agent called "Mark" that outputs markdown from search results; a neural search for personal sites of SF engineers who like information retrieval; a keyword search for a GitHub page; and a combined GitHub agent (one-shot with o3) that first uses neural search to find engineers, extracts names, then keyword-searches for their GitHubs. Bryk closes by announcing a new deep research endpoint launched that day.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Opening and Story Framing
sections.summary: Bryk introduces the talk as a story about web search built for AI, ending with one API to get any information from the web, with coding at the end.

sections.title: 1998: Google and PageRank
sections.summary: Describes Google in 1998 as state-of-the-art information retrieval, using PageRank to rank documents by authority via the web's graph structure, fundamentally still keyword-based.

sections.title: 2021: GPT-3 Insight and Founding Exa
sections.summary: Bryk noticed GPT-3 understood nuanced language while Google failed on 'shirts without stripes.' He committed to building a search engine combining transformer technology with retrieval. Exa joined YC Summer 2021, raised a couple million, spent half on a GPU cluster, and did research for 1.5 years without talking to users.

sections.title: Embeddings vs Keyword Index
sections.summary: Explains the core idea: replace traditional keyword inverted indexes with transformer-generated document embeddings capturing meaning, ideas, and reference patterns. At search time, embed the query and compare to all document embeddings. Training breakthroughs occurred over the research period. Exa successfully returns shirts without stripes for that query.

sections.title: Launch and ChatGPT Disruption
sections.summary: Exa launched November 2022 to excitement on Twitter. Two weeks later ChatGPT launched, initially threatening the premise but ultimately reinforcing that LLMs need external search.

sections.title: Why LLMs Always Need Search
sections.summary: Information-theory argument: GPT-4 weights are under 10 TB while the web is over a million TB (exabyte range). The web also constantly updates. Therefore LLMs will always need external search.

sections.title: Search Built for AI, Not Humans
sections.summary: Traditional search engines were built for lazy humans who type simple keywords and want few clickable links. AI agents carry large accumulated context, use complex multi-constraint queries, and want precise, controllable results. AI needs search engines that handle multi-paragraph queries; Google has a few dozen keyword limit while Exa handles multiple paragraphs.

sections.title: AI Wants Comprehensive Knowledge
sections.summary: AI agents want comprehensive knowledge: they can process 10,000 pages in 3 seconds if parallelized, unlike humans who would need 10 days. A VC wanting all companies in a space needs truly all of them, not just the 10-20 Google returns. Exa can return thousands of results with semantic filtering.

sections.title: Expanding Query Space
sections.summary: Maps the expanding space of possible queries: pre-2022 keyword queries (stripe pricing, GitHub pages, Taylor Swift's boyfriend), post-2022 LLM-style queries (explain like I'm 5, debug my code), semantic queries (people in SF who know assembly), and complex filtered queries (articles arguing X not Y by author Z). This turns the web into a filterable database, which is what AIs want. New query types emerge weekly.

sections.title: Closing the Story: One API
sections.summary: Bryk closes the narrative arc with the same slide: one API to get any information from the web, handling keyword, semantic, and complex queries, eventually all queries. AI plus Exa providing knowledge.

sections.title: Search Dashboard Demo
sections.summary: Bryk navigates technical difficulties switching to the code editor, then demonstrates Exa's search dashboard. Shows toggles for number of results (10, 100, 1000), date ranges, domain filters, and neural vs keyword search modes. Emphasizes that the many toggles are desirable because AI agents call this API and need full control.

sections.title: Agent Mark and Neural Search Demo
sections.summary: Introduces agent.py with 'Mark,' an agent that makes markdown out of anything. Demos a neural search for 'personal site of engineer in San Francisco who likes information retrieval'—a query type where neural search excels over keyword.

sections.title: Keyword Search and Combined GitHub Agent
sections.summary: Demos a keyword search for a GitHub page, suited for traditional Google-like lookup. Then shows a combined GitHub agent one-shot with o3 that first runs neural search to find SF engineers who like information retrieval, extracts names, then keyword-searches for their GitHubs. Returns 10 results, scalable to 1000 on enterprise plans. Argues the right future agent decides which search type to use per subtask.

sections.title: Research Endpoint and Closing
sections.summary: Announces a new research endpoint launched that day, which orchestrates multiple searches and LLM calls in the background to produce deep research reports or structured outputs. Closes the talk.
